topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: vLLM Semantic Router
description: vLLM Semantic Router (arXiv:2510.08731, 'When to Reason: Semantic Router for vLLM', Chen Wang et al., IBM Research / Red Hat / vLLM project, Oct 2025) is an intent-classifying router pushed below the application into the inference-engine / gateway layer via Envoy ext_proc. A ModernBERT classifier (later mmBERT-32K in the Athena release) fine-tuned for multi-task intent classification runs inside a high-performance Rust core built on Hugging Face Candle (zero-copy, SIMD, CPU/GPU inline inference), exposed to Envoy through Go-Rust (CGO) bindings. The pipeline does a semantic-cache check first, then security checks (jailbreak/PII), then intent/complexity classification, model-endpoint selection, and an auto-reasoning ('when to reason') gate that sends simple prompts down a fast path and complex prompts into chain-of-thought / higher reasoning_effort. On MMLU-Pro (Qwen3-30B-A3B on vLLM v0.10.1, NVIDIA L4, TP=4) it reports +10.2pp accuracy, -47.1% latency, -48.5% tokens vs direct vLLM inference. Later releases (Iris v0.1, Athena v0.2) add a signal-driven decision engine (13 signal types composed via Boolean rules), online feedback adaptation from the user's next chat turn (mmBERT-32K Feedback Detector, 98.8% accuracy, <1ms), and multi-provider routing. It defines a new architectural axis: inference-engine/gateway-layer routing vs application-layer routing.
decomposition_method: None — the router does not decompose a compound prompt into sub-tasks. It treats the whole query as a single unit and classifies it (intent/domain, complexity, safety) to choose a model endpoint and reasoning mode. Multi-intent splitting is out of scope; the contribution is per-query classification and gating, not decomposition. [uncertain]
decomposition_granularity: Not applicable — no sub-task splitting. The routed unit is the entire incoming request (one HTTP/chat query) as intercepted at the Envoy gateway. [uncertain]
ordering_strategy: Not applicable — there is no multi-sub-task ordering. Internally the per-request pipeline is a fixed sequence (semantic-cache check -> security/jailbreak/PII checks -> intent+complexity classification -> model-endpoint selection -> auto-reasoning gate), but this is a fixed processing pipeline, not sub-task ordering. [uncertain]
decomposition_validation: Not applicable to decomposition (no decomposition step). The analogous quality control is multi-stage classification run in parallel (category/intent, PII detection, jailbreak detection) plus a semantic-cache hit check and, in later releases, a Boolean decision engine that composes signal conditions into routing policies. No verification of sub-task solvability/completeness/non-redundancy because there are no sub-tasks. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: flat — a single classification + gating decision per request; no milestone/step hierarchy, no skill tree. (The Athena release layers multiple signal types but they feed one flat routing decision.)
router_type: single-label / multi-task classifier gate. A fine-tuned encoder (ModernBERT; mmBERT-32K in Athena) performs intent/domain classification, complexity (reason-or-not) classification, and safety classification; outputs drive a model-endpoint pick and a reasoning on/off (and reasoning_effort/max_tokens) gate. In later releases this is generalized to a signal-driven decision engine that evaluates Boolean formulas over ~13 signal types to select the decision. [uncertain]
routing_model: Separate fine-tuned encoder classifier (not the served generation LLM): ModernBERT (RoPE + FlashAttention, long-context, memory-efficient), fine-tuned multi-task on MMLU-Pro (~12K academic samples / ~14 domains), Microsoft Presidio (~50K token-level PII examples), and jailbreak security datasets. The Athena release upgrades to mmBERT-32K (307M params, 1,800+ languages) with eight neural classifiers. Inference runs in a Rust/Candle core, not the main LLM.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort classification-driven pick. Ambiguous/borderline queries are resolved by the classifier's complexity/intent scores choosing fast-path vs reasoning and a model endpoint; there is no clarification request, abstain, or POMDP-based disambiguation at routing time. In later releases an online feedback signal (user's next turn) can trigger re-routing to a stronger model if the first pick was wrong, an after-the-fact correction rather than upfront disambiguation. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: route to a default/general model endpoint or fall through to standard inference. If no specialized route/cache applies, the request proceeds through normal model selection (and can be re-routed to a stronger model/pool on detected dissatisfaction in later releases). Safety signals (jailbreak/PII) can block/redact rather than route. No human escalation or re-decomposition. [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: Not a skill-pool retriever — the candidate set is a small set of model endpoints / backend clusters (and reasoning modes), not a large skill/tool registry. Selection is by classifier output mapped to a backend cluster via Envoy routing, not embedding top-k retrieval over thousands of skills. Scales by adding endpoints and signal rules, not by skill retrieval. [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Not applicable in the skill-text sense — there is no skill body vs name+description asymmetry. The analogous asymmetry is layer-level: the router (gateway) sees the raw request plus extracted signals (semantics, safety, complexity) and chooses the backend, while the backend model only sees the (possibly modified) request. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: Not an executor of sub-tasks — it is a per-request routing/gating layer in front of inference. For a given request it does sequential pipeline processing (cache -> security -> classify -> select -> gate) then forwards to one backend model; classification sub-stages (category/PII/jailbreak) run in parallel within the Rust core. [uncertain]
parallel_vs_concurrent: The Rust/Candle core runs multi-stage classification (category, PII, jailbreak) concurrently/in parallel using Rust's thread-safe ownership model for low-latency inline inference; this is concurrency within the router's classification, not parallel tool-call execution. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: Not applicable — no sub-tasks and therefore no inter-sub-task dependency analysis. Routing is a single per-request decision. [uncertain]
result_aggregation: Not applicable — a single backend produces the response; the router does not merge results from multiple sub-tasks. Semantic-cache hits short-circuit and return a cached response directly. [uncertain]
mid_chain_feedback: soft/hard across turns (later releases). Within a single request there is no re-planning. Across a multi-turn session, the mmBERT-32K Feedback Detector classifies the user's next turn (satisfied / needs clarification / wrong answer / wants different approach, 98.8% accuracy, <1ms) and re-routes subsequent turns to a stronger model or different pool — a hard re-routing loop driven by implicit feedback rather than a within-request re-plan. [uncertain]
benchmark_name: MMLU-Pro (primary; 14 domains) for the core paper, measuring accuracy, token usage, and latency. Training/eval data also includes Microsoft Presidio (PII) and jailbreak security datasets. Later releases add internal benchmarks for feedback detection, hallucination/fact-checking, and PII classifiers.
multi_intent_coverage: Single-intent per request. MMLU-Pro questions are single academic queries; the benchmark measures whether to reason and which domain/model, not compound multi-intent decomposition. No explicit parallel/sequential multi-intent categories. [uncertain]
accuracy_metric: outcome-style: downstream task accuracy on MMLU-Pro (final-answer correctness) as the headline metric, jointly reported with latency and token-consumption reductions. Classifier-side metrics (e.g., feedback-detector accuracy 98.8%) are reported for individual signal modules. The reasoning gate is judged by net effect on answer accuracy vs cost, not by routing exact-match.
clarification_capability: Partially, indirectly. The core paper does not model when-to-ask vs when-to-answer. The Athena feedback detector includes a 'needs clarification' class among its four labels for the user's next turn, but this is post-hoc dissatisfaction classification driving re-routing, not a generated clarification question or a when-to-ask benchmark like ClarifyBench/InteractComp. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: outcome-only — evaluated on final MMLU-Pro answer accuracy plus latency/token cost; no process-supervision scoring of intermediate reasoning steps.
eval_stability: Reproducible offline-ish: fixed local model (Qwen3-30B-A3B) served by a pinned vLLM v0.10.1 on fixed hardware (NVIDIA L4, TP=4) over the static MMLU-Pro set, so not subject to external live-API drift; numbers depend on the chosen served model/version. Open-source code aids reproduction. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: inference-engine-layer / gateway: a Go-based Envoy ExtProc (ext_proc) filter intercepts each HTTP request, forwards it via gRPC to an external processor that runs the Rust/Candle classification core (statically linked CGO), and returns the routing decision (backend cluster + reasoning mode) before the request reaches the model. Deploys natively on Kubernetes / service meshes / API gateways (Red Hat OpenShift).
routing_layer: inference-engine-layer / gateway-layer — this is the defining contribution and the new architectural axis: classification and routing are pushed below the application into Envoy ext_proc rather than living in app code or a LangGraph node, affecting latency, semantic caching, and isolation.
latency_overhead: Very low and net-negative overall. Classification runs in milliseconds (feedback/signal classifiers <1ms; multi-stage parallel inline inference in Rust/Candle); statically-linked CGO minimizes runtime overhead. The routing+gating step adds small per-request cost but yields net -47.1% response latency and -48.5% tokens on MMLU-Pro by avoiding unnecessary reasoning (later release reports up to ~5x token saving / ~20% of original token usage at equal accuracy).
online_adaptation: Yes (in later releases). The Athena v0.2 self-learning loop uses reverse/response-side signals and routing outcomes to iteratively improve signal and decision rules; the mmBERT-32K Feedback Detector turns the user's next chat turn into an implicit reward (no separate reward model) to re-route future turns session-aware. Roadmap adds RL-driven selection and ML methods (KNN/KMeans/MLP/SVM/matrix factorization, Elo, RouterDC, AutoMix). The original paper's classifier itself is trained offline/static.
adoption: open-source and production. vLLM project / Red Hat OpenShift integration; experimental launch Sep 2025, v0.1 'Iris' (Jan 2026) first production-ready release, v0.2 'Athena' (Mar 2026). Active community (600+ PRs, 300+ issues, 50+ contributors). Deployed in production as an Envoy external processor; cloud-native Kubernetes deployment. arXiv:2510.08731 paper plus follow-on vision/architecture papers.
